title: What Happens When You Yawn, and Why Is It Contagious?
sources: Cleveland Clinic, 'Yawning' ('Yawning is the opening of your airway and mouth to take a long, deep breath of air'; the lower jaw opens in a 'gaping' of the mouth; 'Adults yawn about nine times a day on average'; the old main theory was that yawning brings in more oxygen, abandoned because a controlled lack of oxygen did not produce more yawning; brain-cooling theory: 'brain temperature decreases with yawning'; 'we're much more likely to have contagious yawning when we see or hear a close loved one yawn as opposed to a stranger'; talk to a provider about excessive yawning over a few days): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/yawning

Provine, Tate & Geldmacher, 'Yawning: no effect of 3-5% CO2, 100% O2, and exercise', Behavioral and Neural Biology 1987;48:382-393 (no support for yawning as a response to high CO2 or low O2; intro: 'Yawns are easily triggered; even reading about or thinking about yawns stimulates them'): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3120687/

Gallup & Eldakar, 'Contagious yawning and seasonal climate variation', Frontiers in Evolutionary Neuroscience 2011 and Gallup's brain-cooling work (yawning framed as a brain-cooling HYPOTHESIS, hence 'one theory ... may'): https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnevo.2011.00007/full

Reissland, Francis & Mason, 'Development of Fetal Yawn Compared with Non-Yawn Mouth Openings from 24-36 Weeks Gestation', PLOS ONE 2012 (4D scans of 15 fetuses show true yawns in the womb, from 24 weeks): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3503956

Helt, Eigsti, Snyder & Fein, 'Contagious Yawning in Autistic and Typical Development', Child Development 2010, via UConn Today (contagious yawning 'doesn't appear in most typically developing children until they are about four years old'; 'None of the 20 one-year-olds in the study yawned; only one in 20 two-year-olds yawned; and two three-year-olds'): https://today.uconn.edu/2010/09/when-yawning-isnt-contagious

Joly-Mascheroni, Senju & Shepherd, 'Dogs catch human yawns', Biology Letters 2008;4(5):446-448 ('Twenty-one dogs yawned when they observed a human yawning' out of 29; control mouth movements elicited no yawns; later studies replicated it only weakly, hence 'might'): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2610100

Norscia & Palagi, 'Yawn Contagion and Empathy in Homo sapiens', PLoS ONE 2011 (contagion greatest for kin, then friends, acquaintances, strangers; used for the director's background detail only): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3233580

Tease (next video): NHS, 'Heartburn and acid reflux' ('Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat (acid reflux)'): https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heartburn-and-acid-reflux/

lines.text: You yawned in the womb, but catching yawns starts at age one, or four?
lines.caps: YOU *YAWNED | IN THE *WOMB | BUT *CATCHING | YAWNS *STARTS | AT AGE *ONE | OR *FOUR?

lines.text: Your jaw drops and you gulp one long, deep breath.
lines.caps: YOUR JAW *DROPS | AND YOU *GULP | ONE *LONG | DEEP *BREATH

lines.text: Not for oxygen; tests ruled that out.
One theory? It may cool your brain.
But here's the weird part: just reading about yawns can trigger one.
lines.caps: BUT *HERE'S | THE *WEIRD PART | JUST *READING | ABOUT *YAWNS | CAN *TRIGGER ONE

lines.text: Feel one coming yet? Thought so.
Answer: about age four. Toddlers rarely do.
Your dog might too. One study: twenty-one of twenty-nine.
